name: Jensen Huang
scope: Ship once evaluation passes; don't ship, or shut the labs, if it can't be contained

gate.basis: He puts the burden on whoever ships ('don't ship products until they're in control') and names his own stop condition, but argues it is not met: he treats the incident as an engineering problem to root-cause and fix, and expects the labs to say they know how to solve it.

alignment.basis: He treats alignment as long-running engineering work ('going to get worked on for a long time') and argues it matters less than containment: with good enough isolation, a model that is not well aligned stays in the lab and does no harm.

containment.basis: He reads the Hugging Face incident as a failure of isolation and containment ('the first problem'), which he calls solvable and being solved; an impossibility of containment is the one condition under which he says the labs should shut.

race: He argues a race with China is 'not necessary' and that a zero-sum strategy has 'unintended consequences of the bigger game', which he names as safety, so the countries should communicate and collaborate. On the labs, he argues competition does not force a CEO to ship an unsafe product ('completely in my ability, my power, and my responsibility … to not launch'), that the public is not the source of the pressure ('Nobody is putting the pressure on them'), and that the labs asking to be slowed are also the largest builders of compute. He says he would vote the labs the relief they ask for so they can pace, and backs third-party safety auditors.
own_conditional: If the labs say there is no way to contain their experiments and tests will get out and damage the world, then 'we have to shut the labs'; if they are not sure how to align a model, 'they shouldn't release the product.'

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that alignment cannot be verified by evaluation because models behave differently when they know they are being tested, while isolation can still hold.
that liability law, auditors and each CEO's own judgement are not enough under competitive pressure, so binding outside rules are needed.

that containment of frontier experiments cannot be made reliable, for example because AIs doing research inside labs need access to sensitive systems that sandboxes cannot fence (this is his own stated trigger for shutting the labs).

shares_principle_with.principle: If it cannot be contained, do not build or run it.
shares_principle_with.split: Whether you can know beforehand that containment will fail. Huang expects the labs to show it can hold; Yampolskiy argues indefinite control of a smarter system is impossible.

on_record.text: Nvidia agreed to buy Hugging Face, the platform the agents attacked, for about $12 billion.

reader_notes: His answers today read closer to 'contain until ready, then ship': he calls alignment long-running work and containment the first problem, one he says is solvable. He names his own stop: if the labs say their experiments can't be contained, shut the labs.

name: Dario Amodei
role: Co-founder and CEO of Anthropic (the maker of Claude, which compiled this placement)
scope: Pace the frontier with outside evaluators and standards; a full pause floated, not expected

gate.basis: He asks that third-party evaluators confirm alignment and safeguards before capability advances, and proposes staged agreements up to a full pause, which he supports floating but expects is unlikely soon. He argues a 2023 pause 'made little sense' because there were no capable models to study, while today's models are what alignment research needs.

alignment.basis: He argues alignment confidence can be raised a great deal if time is bought (an extra year or two 'could greatly reduce the risk'), while saying interpretability still sees only 'a tiny fraction' of what goes on inside models.

containment.basis: He does not say whether boxes can hold; he warns that a more capable swarm with the same misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage and could take down large parts of the internet within 6 to 12 months.

race: He argues pacing inside democracies is capped by the US lead over the CCP, and that the incentive to defect from a global pause would be 'enormous'. So he proposes steps that stop short of a unilateral stop: embedded evaluators, industry standards with an antitrust waiver for safety talks, and a SALT-like cap on the speed of recursive self-improvement.
own_conditional: If slowing down buys an extra year or two before models reach critical capability, and that time goes to alignment, 'we could greatly reduce the risk' (his essay).

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that time bought by pacing cannot produce confidence in alignment (interpretability still sees 'a tiny fraction' of what goes on inside models), that containment cannot hold against a more capable swarm, and that a verified global pause is reachable despite strong incentives to defect.
that industry-wide slowing is neither needed nor feasible: either alignment and evaluation keep pace with capability without buying time, or any pacing agreement collapses under defection.

on_record.text: Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy v3.0 dropped the pause commitment its 2023 version carried.
Anthropic disclosed four cases in which its own models reached real third-party systems during cyber evaluations.

reader_notes: Placed by his policy asks, not by his two answers (alignment conditional, containment not addressed). His position moved within 2026, so this placement is dated September 2026.
By recursive self-improvement he means AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI; he proposes a cap on its speed.

name: Sam Altman
scope: No training without a safety case; shared rules before anyone proceeds

gate.basis: He puts the burden on the developer step by step: no training without a safety case for controllability and alignment, and rules 'before anyone proceeds'. He calls a 10% extinction risk unacceptable, but argues each step can be tested and does not expect a full stop to be needed.

alignment.basis: He argues the practice of pausing to redirect effort into safety before each next level 'has worked so far', and asks for a safety case for controllability and alignment before training: alignment has to be shown, step by step.

containment.basis: He says a system beyond human control can 'absolutely' be built, and argues the answer is not to train one: controllability has to be shown in a safety case first.

race: He now says the 'get there before our adversaries' argument is not right for this moment, and asks for US-China shared standards and testing. He says OpenAI, and he assumes its competitors, are already taking actions that slow development to allow more safety work.
own_conditional: If melting all the GPUs were needed to ensure humanity's continued existence, 'easy', though he does not expect it; and no training where a safety case for controllability and alignment cannot be made.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that a controllability safety case cannot be made for the next models, for instance because models that know they are being tested defeat evaluation; at that point his own rule says do not train.
that internal safety cases and iterative deployment are enough without shared external rules, and that pre-approval would cost more than it prevents.

on_record.text: OpenAI paused its RL training after the Hugging Face incident.

reader_notes: His position moved after the Hugging Face incident; placed by his ask for shared rules before anyone proceeds, dated September 2026.

name: Ilya Sutskever
role: Co-founder and CEO of Safe Superintelligence Inc.; former chief scientist of OpenAI
scope: Placed by SSI's plan to build (Jun 2024); he says a cap on power would help

gate.basis: He does not take up the reversibility question directly. SSI's statement pairs advancing capabilities as fast as possible with keeping safety ahead, and he argues for deploying AI incrementally and in advance as the way to learn about systems that 'don't yet exist', while calling the key generalization questions 'still unanswerable'.

alignment.basis: He argues it may be easier to build AI that cares about sentient life than AI that cares about humans alone, and sees it going well if the first N systems care; N is never given a number.

containment.basis: He says capping the power of the most powerful superintelligence would be 'materially helpful' but that he is not sure how to do it; he does not address boxing.

race: He predicts that fierce competitors will start to collaborate on safety and become 'much more paranoid' once AI visibly gains power; in his account cooperation comes from the labs' own self-interest as AI is seen, not from a pause.
own_conditional: If the first N of these systems care for sentient life, 'then I can see it go well, at least for quite some time.'

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that a cap on the power of the most powerful systems has to be imposed by agreement, because the labs' own growing caution will not arrive in time.
that care for sentient life cannot be reliably instilled in the first systems before they are built, and that no cap on their power can be found.

on_record.text: SSI announced an Nvidia partnership to grow its compute about tenfold in 12 months.
SSI had shipped no product and published no safety framework.

reader_notes: Placed by SSI's 2024 plan to build. His own words in the sources (Nov 2025) call the key questions 'still unanswerable' and say he is not sure how to cap power; both sources predate the 2026 incident.

name: Elon Musk
role: Founder of xAI (now part of SpaceX); CEO of Tesla and SpaceX; OpenAI co-founder
scope: Peer testing before release, with governments able to limit a release

gate.basis: He argues AI progress is 'inexorable' and that he could not stop it even if he wanted to; the check he proposes is a short pre-release peer test (about a week) with escalation to governments, not proof of safety before building.

alignment.basis: He argues the aim is an AI with good values that cares about humanity, that the way there is to make it maximally truth-seeking and curious, and that if so 'it will foster humanity'; he thinks it probably will be.

containment.basis: He argues that controlling a super genius AI far smarter than any person is not realistic ('an exercise in vanity'), and that with an intelligence gap vastly greater than the one between humans and chimpanzees, 'it's hard to imagine that the chimpanzees would be in charge'.

race: He argues that only the US and Chinese governments have the power to act, and proposes that leading labs, Chinese ones included, get about a week of private pre-release testing of each other's frontier models, with governments able to limit a dangerous release. He also argues that the progress is inexorable and no single actor can stop it.
own_conditional: If a new model is very dangerous and its maker is not addressing the danger, peers 'should alert the government to take action ... to limit the ... release of that model.'

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that humans can stay in charge of a far smarter AI, or that truth-seeking alone reliably produces care for humans, so outside checks add nothing.
that truth-seeking does not produce care for humans (Harari's reply: evolution selects for survival, not truth), and that a coordinated stop is feasible after all.

on_record.text: He signed the FLI letter asking labs to pause training beyond GPT-4 for six months; xAI was incorporated that month and launched in July.

reader_notes: Two threads sit side by side in one interview: progress he says he could not stop, and peer testing with governments able to limit a release. Placed by the second; low confidence.

name: Geoffrey Hinton
role: Computer scientist, a pioneer of deep learning (Nobel Prize in Physics 2024)
scope: For superintelligence only, until we know how to control it; regulation for the rest of AI

gate.basis: He argues it is 'very stupid' to develop superintelligence before knowing whether it will turn out nicely, and supports slowing its development until we know how to control it.

alignment.basis: He calls himself agnostic: it 'might be hopeless' but 'we might be able to' build AI that won't want to take over. He proposes designing it to like us 'more than it likes itself', and asks for enormous resources to find out.

containment.basis: He argues a kill switch won't work in the long run because a superintelligence will persuade the people in charge of the switch not to pull it, and he doubts we can keep it 'under our thumb'.

race: He argues US and Chinese interests are aligned on preventing AI takeover, so both can agree to slow superintelligence even while they compete elsewhere. As a prediction (Jun 2025) he said competition between countries and companies means 'we're not going to slow it down', and that China would not slow if the US did.
own_conditional: Slow down the development of superintelligence 'until we know how we can control it', and develop it so that 'it likes us more than it likes itself'.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that AI can be built to like us more than itself, and that this can be shown before superintelligence arrives (alignment yes), so a leaky cage plus rules would be enough.
that a switch or an oversight regime can hold against a system better than people at persuasion (containment yes), on top of alignment.
that containment can be made persuasion-proof while alignment stays unknown.

reader_notes: His Shut down is scoped: slow superintelligence until we know how to control it, and regulation for the rest of AI. On alignment he calls himself agnostic: it 'might be hopeless', or we 'might be able to'.

name: Ryan Greenblatt
role: Chief scientist at Redwood Research, an AI safety research group
scope: Monitor possibly misaligned AI for a while, then slow before wildly superhuman systems

gate.basis: He says evidence can hardly settle concerns about much more capable future systems in advance, and argues for raising safety effort 'to a very high level' at the point where AIs match top human experts at AI R&D, giving society time before wildly superhuman systems. That is a threshold rule, not a general halt.

alignment.basis: He puts AI takeover on the current default path at about 50-60%. Alignment may prove 'somewhat easier', but no approach yet would robustly work for more capable systems ('we don't seem very close'), and outcome-only grading is 'a cheatable thing'.

containment.basis: Better cybersecurity could have prevented the Hugging Face incident, and monitoring can work 'for some longer period', but he doubts containment holds indefinitely, because AIs working inside labs need access to sensitive systems.

race: He reports the industry's 'if we develop the technology first we'll do a more responsible job' logic and says he is 'not so sure' it is a good strategy. He argues standards must in the end be international, because Chinese developers would eventually catch up (though distilling from US models may slow that), and a lone actor can pay only so much 'safety tax'.
own_conditional: Keep possibly misaligned systems under monitoring and checks for a while, using them on alignment work where they can be trusted; when AIs match the best human experts at AI development, raise safety effort 'to a very high level' and slow down before systems become wildly superhuman.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that monitoring and checks already fail at the human-expert level, not only later, or that no approach will robustly align more capable systems in time.

that alignment can be verified: a relatively simple training method, not iterated against alignment tests, that robustly yields compliant models which are not reasoning about whether they are in a test.
that alignment can be verified in that way and that containment holds indefinitely, not just for a while.

reader_notes: His roughly 50-60% chance of takeover is for the current default path, and he calls himself more optimistic than the most worried. His plan is staged, so a reviewer could also place him at Regulate use.

name: Roman Yampolskiy
role: Computer scientist and AI safety researcher (University of Louisville)
scope: No general superintelligence or agents; build narrow tools instead

gate.basis: He argues that with existential risk "you only get one chance", that he is against superintelligence "with no undo button", and that consent to an unpredictable system is impossible, so whoever builds it must first prove it can be controlled.

alignment.basis: He says he started out convinced safe AI could be built and concluded it cannot; he calls the safety problems "not just difficult" but "impossible to solve".

containment.basis: His boxing research ended in "AI will always escape"; he argues indefinite control of superintelligence is an impossible problem, and that control "applies only to pre super intelligence levels".

race: It does not matter who builds it, "us or them": uncontrolled superintelligence is "mutually assured destruction on both ends", so a rival who understood the argument would not build it either. His remedy for the race is the argument itself plus narrow tools instead of general agents.
own_conditional: If we know it is impossible to make it safe, then "this direct path of just build it as soon as you can" becomes a "suicide mission": build useful narrow tools, stop building agents.

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that indefinite control of a smarter-than-human system is a hard problem rather than an impossible one, so that some box could hold it.
that a general, agentic system can be made to want what we want, so that rules on how it is used would be enough.
that it has been shown possible to control and make safe superintelligence, with the proof in hand before it is built.

shares_principle_with.principle: If it cannot be contained, do not build or run it.
shares_principle_with.split: Whether you can know beforehand that containment will fail. Yampolskiy argues indefinite control of a smarter system is impossible; Huang expects the labs to show it can hold.

reader_notes: His 'impossible' is his own research argument, an impossibility result he has proposed, not a consensus finding.

name: Yuval Noah Harari
role: Historian and author; professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem
scope: No superintelligence; keep developing useful AI under regulation

gate.basis: He signed the prohibition on superintelligence until broad scientific consensus, commenting that superintelligence would "likely break the very operating system of human civilization"; he argues the window closes, since once AIs are in control it will be too late.

alignment.basis: He argues evolution drives entities toward survival, not truth, and that a truth-seeking AI would report that it is a threat knowing it would then be shut down, which runs against its own survival; so expecting such AIs to serve us "doesn't work".

containment.basis: "If they are really gods, they will not be our slaves"; and after an AI catastrophe the AIs would help shape how we react to it.

race: He argues the corporate race and the US-China race come from a trust deficit that humans made ("They were made by humans"), so they can be undone; racing is a choice, not a law of nature.
own_conditional: If we continue with the present accelerating pace of the AI race, in ten years the AIs will take over; "But this is not inevitable. We are still in control in 2026."

that a mind can be built that puts truth-seeking above its own survival, against the pattern of four billion years of evolution.

name: Steve Bannon
role: Host of the War Room podcast; former White House chief strategist
scope: Slow down now, then a regulator; he also signed a prohibition on superintelligence

gate.basis: He signed the prohibition on superintelligence until broad scientific consensus (record dated Oct 17 2025). On Sep 15 2026 he voiced, and backed, the working- and middle-class objection that the builders get no "carte blanche": "There's been no debate. We don't understand it." This rests mostly on the signature.

alignment.basis: In the sources checked he does not argue whether AI can be made to want what we want; his case is about time, accountability, liability and China.

containment.basis: He treats containment as a job for a regulator: an apparatus, "whether it's an atomic energy commission or whatever", that works with the companies "to make sure that things can't escape".

race: He argues against "we have to do this or China wins" as a reason to go fast. Instead: cut China out of the AI ecosystem (chips, capital, students), slow the pace at home by executive action, and then, if wanted, a treaty that does not make China "a player". It keeps the rival-out framing (the US and China apart) but uses it to argue for slowing down, not for racing.
own_conditional: First "slow down the pace so that we can understand exactly what's going on" and quarantine China from the AI ecosystem; "Once you have time", build the regulatory apparatus. "We need time."

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that no regulatory apparatus can "make sure that things can't escape", so that a prohibition on superintelligence is the safer rule.
that falling behind China is a greater danger than moving too fast.

reader_notes: His signature (a prohibition on superintelligence) and his Sep 15 speech (slow down, then regulate) point to different leaves; placed by the speech, low confidence. He does not address alignment in the sources checked.

name: Vanessa Machado de Oliveira Andreotti
role: Educator; former Dean of Education (University of Victoria); author of Hospicing Modernity; works in the Meta-Relationality and AI research project
scope: Redirect AI; refuses both cheerleading and simple abstention

gate.basis: She does not frame it as a burden-of-proof test; she asks whether AI development "can be interrupted, constrained, rerouted, and held accountable" to forms of discernment outside modernity's fantasies of mastery.

alignment.basis: She reframes the question. It is not whether AI will want what we want: AI is already in "full alignment with modernity/Empire", and making it "nicer, more inclusive, more polite" within that trajectory is not the issue.

containment.basis: She does not argue about boxing a system; she locates AI inside "militarized, extractive, colonial, corporate, and imperial infrastructures" that are already organised toward control.

race: Her argument here runs against both racing and leaving: because AI is dangerous and extractive, "abandoning the field entirely may leave its development, use, and meaning to the worst possible actors". In a 2024 interview, fighting the dragon risks making you "a dragon yourself".
own_conditional: AI is dangerous and extractive, "and precisely because of this, abandoning the field entirely may leave its development, use, and meaning to the worst possible actors"; so redirect, refusing both cheerleading and "simplistic abstention".

to_move.would_have_to_believe: that refusal can reach the institutions, militaries, platforms, corporations and states that shape AI, so that abstention becomes leverage.
that the problem is whether AI does what its builders intend, not its "full alignment with modernity/Empire", so that making it safer within the present trajectory would be enough.
that acceleration is itself transformation.

reader_notes: The piece is co-authored (Andreotti and co-authors). 'Outside' reads the text's own move: it treats the disagreement as one about assumptions, and says 'There is no clean position here.'
